title: Recursion vs Loops
concept: When solving the same problem with recursion and loops, memory usage is completely different

steps.title: Including header file
steps.explanation:
We include the standard I/O library with **`#include <stdio.h>`** to use `printf`.

This lesson answers an important question: **"What's the difference between solving the same problem with recursion vs a loop?"** We implement the sum from 1 to n in both ways and compare **memory usage**.

steps.title: Calling sum_recursive(5) from main
steps.explanation: **`printf("Recursive: %d\n", sum_recursive(5));`** -- Computes 1+2+3+4+5 **recursively**. `sum_recursive(5) = 5 + sum_recursive(4)`, breaking the problem down as "sum up to 5 = 5 + sum up to 4".

steps.title: Recursion: stack frames pile up to 6 layers
steps.explanation: **`return n + sum_recursive(n - 1);`** -- From sum_recursive(5) to sum_recursive(0), a total of 6 calls are made, so including main, **7 frames** exist simultaneously. Each frame uses approximately 16-32 bytes of memory.

steps.title: Recursive result: 15
steps.explanation: Starting from the base case, return values propagate in reverse: sum_recursive(0)=**0** -> (1)=1+0=**1** -> (2)=2+1=**3** -> (3)=3+3=**6** -> (4)=4+6=**10** -> (5)=5+10=**15**. All frames are popped and the final result `15` is returned to main.

steps.title: Loop: calling sum_loop(5)
steps.explanation: **`printf("Loop: %d\n", sum_loop(5));`** -- Now we solve the same problem with a **loop (for loop)**. Only **one** sum_loop frame is created, and since it does not call itself, no additional frames are pushed.

steps.title: Loop: variable values change and accumulate
steps.explanation: **`total += i;`** -- Instead of creating new frames, it computes by **changing variable values within the same frame**: when i=1 total=1, i=2 total=3, i=3 total=6, i=4 total=10, i=5 total=15. When `i` becomes 6, the condition `i <= n` (6 <= 5) is false and the loop ends.

steps.title: Final comparison: recursion vs loop
steps.explanation: Both methods produce the same result of `15`, but memory usage is **worlds apart**. Recursion uses **n+1 frames** (O(n)), while the loop uses just **1 frame** (O(1)).

quiz.question: What problem is most likely to occur when calling sum_recursive(10000)?
options: It works fine without any issues
quiz.explanation:
sum_recursive(10000) creates 10,001 stack frames.
With a typical stack size (1-8MB), handling this many frames may be difficult, causing a Stack Overflow.
In contrast, sum_loop(10000) uses only 1 frame and works without any issues.

misconceptions.wrong: Recursion and loops use the same amount of memory
misconceptions.correct: Recursion uses memory proportional to the call depth, while loops use a fixed amount of memory.
misconceptions.why: Recursion creates a new stack frame per call requiring O(n) memory, but loops reuse the same variables requiring only O(1).

misconceptions.wrong: What loops can do, recursion cannot
misconceptions.correct: Every loop can be converted to recursion, and every recursion can be converted to a loop.
misconceptions.why: Mathematically, both approaches have equivalent expressive power. The difference lies in code readability and efficiency.

keyTakeaway: Recursion is concise but piles up stack frames using more memory. A loop needs only one frame. Choose the method that fits the nature of the problem.
